claim: Skeletal muscle satellite cells in their niche are quiescent.
source: Skeletal muscle satellite cells in their niche are quiescent and upon muscle injury, exit quiescence, proliferate to repair muscle tissue, and self-renew to replenish the satellite cell population.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by the citation to Schultz, 1976 in the Introduction.

claim: Upon muscle injury, satellite cells exit quiescence, proliferate to repair muscle tissue, and self-renew to replenish the satellite cell population.
source: Skeletal muscle satellite cells in their niche are quiescent and upon muscle injury, exit quiescence, proliferate to repair muscle tissue, and self-renew to replenish the satellite cell population.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Transcripts encoding RNA binding proteins were among the most significantly changed during satellite cell activation following muscle injury.
source: Transcripts encoding RNA binding proteins were among the most significantly changed and included the mRNA decay factor Tristetraprolin.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data analysis presented in Figure 1 and described in the Results section.

claim: Tristetraprolin promotes the decay of MyoD mRNA via binding to the MyoD mRNA 3′ untranslated region.
source: Tristetraprolin promotes the decay of MyoD mRNA, which encodes a transcriptional regulator of myogenic commitment, via binding to the MyoD mRNA 3′ untranslated region.
evidence: This is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation assays (Figure 4A) and mRNA decay assays (Figure 4C,D) presented in the manuscript.

claim: Upon satellite cell activation, p38α/β MAPK phosphorylates MAPKAP2 and inactivates Tristetraprolin, stabilizing MyoD mRNA.
source: Upon satellite cell activation, p38α/β MAPK phosphorylates MAPKAP2 and inactivates Tristetraprolin, stabilizing MyoD mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by proximity ligation assays showing phospho-MK2::TTP association (Figure 3C,D) and experiments with MK2 inhibitors (Figure 3E).

claim: Satellite cell specific knockdown of Tristetraprolin precociously activates satellite cells in vivo.
source: Satellite cell specific knockdown of Tristetraprolin precociously activates satellite cells in vivo, enabling MyoD accumulation, differentiation and cell fusion into myofibers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RCAS-mediated shRNA knockdown experiments showing increased MyoD+ cells and mCherry+ fibers (Figure 5D-F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).

claim: Quiescent satellite cells possess minimal cytoplasm, condensed chromatin, and few ribosomes.
source: Skeletal muscle satellite cells (SCs) are maintained as a quiescent stem cell population (Schultz, 1976) possessing minimal cytoplasm, condensed chromatin, and few ribosomes (Wakayama et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wakayama et al., 1979.

claim: Upon muscle injury, satellite cells activate and then enter S-phase to generate a proliferating myoblast population.
source: Upon muscle injury, SCs activate and then enter S-phase to generate a proliferating myoblast population that differentiates, repairs skeletal muscle tissue, and self-renews to replenish the stem cell pool (Cornelison et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cornelison et al., 2001.

claim: Induction of MyoD is a critical component of the satellite cell activation cascade.
source: Induction of MyoD, a myogenic regulatory transcription factor, is a critical component of this activation cascade.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: The p38α/β MAPK pathway is activated immediately upon satellite cell activation, prior to MyoD induction.
source: Prior to MyoD induction, and immediately upon satellite cell activation, the p38α/β MAPK pathway is activated, serving as a molecular switch (Jones et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jones et al., 2005.

claim: In a subset of satellite cells, p38α/β is asymmetrically activated during cell division to promote satellite cell self-renewal and re-acquisition of quiescence.
source: In a subset of SCs, p38α/β is asymmetrically activated during cell division to promote SC self-renewal and re-acquisition of quiescence (Troy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Troy et al., 2012.

claim: Aged satellite cells exhibit an intrinsic self-renewal deficit that arises in part from a failure to asymmetrically activate p38α/β MAPK.
source: Moreover, aged SCs exhibit an intrinsic self-renewal deficit that arises in part from a failure to asymmetrically activate p38α/β MAPK (Bernet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bernet et al., 2014.

claim: Post-transcriptional gene regulatory mechanisms, including translational repression, contribute to satellite cell activation and play a key role in the maintenance of the quiescent satellite cell state.
source: Importantly, post-transcriptional gene regulatory mechanisms, including translational repression, contribute to SC activation and play a key role in the maintenance of the quiescent SC state (Crist et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crist et al., 2012.

claim: TTP binds to AU-rich elements within the 3′ untranslated region of target transcripts and recruits deadenylases, initiating mRNA decay.
source: TTP (Tristetraprolin), a target of the p38α/β MAPK pathway, binds to AU-rich elements within the 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTR) of target transcripts and recruits deadenylases, initiating mRNA decay (Lai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lai et al., 2000.

claim: Rates of mRNA decay fluctuate depending on cellular conditions and are controlled by specialized mRNA binding proteins.
source: Rates of mRNA decay, which fluctuate depending on cellular conditions, are controlled by specialized mRNA binding proteins (RBPs) that bind target mRNAs and activate cellular mRNA decay enzymes (Parker and Song, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parker and Song, 2004.

claim: The Tis11 gene family is comprised of four genes: Zfp36 (TTP), Zfp36l1, Zfp36l2 and Zfp36l3.
source: TTP is the best studied of the four member Tis11 gene family, which is comprised of the genes: Zfp36 (TTP), Zfp36l1, Zfp36l2 and Zfp36l3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the gene family.

claim: In macrophages, TTP suppresses the inflammation response by destabilizing proinflammatory mRNAs until extracellular stimuli activate p38α/β MAPK.
source: In macrophages, TTP suppresses the inflammation response by destabilizing proinflammatory mRNAs until extracellular stimuli activate p38α/β MAPK (Stumpo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stumpo et al., 2010.

claim: The p38α/β MAPK signaling pathway phosphorylates TTP, promoting association with 14-3-3 adaptor proteins and blocking the recruitment of deadenylases, thereby stabilizing transcripts with TTP 3′ UTR binding sites.
source: The p38α/β MAPK signaling pathway then phosphorylates TTP, promoting association with 14-3-3 adaptor proteins and blocking the recruitment of deadenylases, thereby stabilizing transcripts with TTP 3′ UTR binding sites (Clement et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clement et al., 2011.

claim: TTP loss-of-function is associated with a severe inflammatory syndrome caused by chronic over-expression of Tumor Necrosis Factor α mRNA.
source: TTP loss-of-function has profound effects on overall organismal health and is associated with a severe inflammatory syndrome caused by chronic over-expression of Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF)α mRNA, as loss of TNF receptor function largely rescues TTP KO phenotypes in TTP/TNFR1/2 triple knockout mice (Carballo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Carballo et al., 2001.

claim: Transcripts encoding TTP family members are among the fastest declining and dynamically regulated mRNAs following satellite cell activation.
source: Transcripts encoding TTP family members are among the fastest declining and dynamically regulated mRNAs following SC activation, where the transcripts initially decline and then are re-expressed (Farina et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Farina et al., 2012.

claim: 47% of genes in the WT-S4 gene list decreased in expression during satellite cell activation.
source: An unexpectedly high percentage of genes in this list decreased in expression during SC activation (47%), with 'nucleic acid binding: RNA binding,' (GO:0003723; p-value = 8.7e-05) as the most significantly overrepresented gene ontology (GO) term (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on microarray data analysis presented in Figure 1.

claim: 'Nucleic acid binding: RNA binding' (GO:0003723) is the most significantly overrepresented gene ontology term in the WT-S4 gene list with a p-value of 8.7e-05.
source: An unexpectedly high percentage of genes in this list decreased in expression during SC activation (47%), with 'nucleic acid binding: RNA binding,' (GO:0003723; p-value = 8.7e-05) as the most significantly overrepresented gene ontology (GO) term (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis of microarray data.

claim: Zfp36 transcript levels decline precipitously upon wild type satellite cell activation.
source: One of these decay factors, Zfp36, which encodes TTP, declines precipitously upon wild type SC activation (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown by microarray and QT-PCR data in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Transcripts for Zfp36l1 and Zfp36l2, which encode Brf1 and Brf2, respectively, decrease during satellite cell activation.
source: Additionally, transcripts for two other TTP family members, Zfp36l1 and Zfp36l2, which encode Brf1 and Brf2, respectively, also decrease during SC activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Elavl1, which encodes HuR, a MyoD mRNA-stabilizing protein, is up-regulated upon satellite cell activation.
source: Among the minority of transcripts that are up-regulated upon SC activation are genes with known roles in myogenesis, including Elavl1, which encodes HuR, a MyoD mRNA-stabilizing protein (Figure 1E,F) (Figueroa et al., 2003), consistent with the induction of MyoD, which occurs as early as 3 hr following isolation of myofiber-associated SCs (Cornelison et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E,F and supported by citations to Figueroa et al., 2003, Cornelison et al., 2004, and Jones et al., 2005.

claim: MyoD induction occurs as early as 3 hr following isolation of myofiber-associated satellite cells.
source: Among the minority of transcripts that are up-regulated upon SC activation are genes with known roles in myogenesis, including Elavl1, which encodes HuR, a MyoD mRNA-stabilizing protein (Figure 1E,F) (Figueroa et al., 2003), consistent with the induction of MyoD, which occurs as early as 3 hr following isolation of myofiber-associated SCs (Cornelison et al., 2004; Jones et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cornelison et al., 2004 and Jones et al., 2005.

claim: Unphosphorylated, active TTP protein is short-lived as TTP targets its own mRNA for rapid decay.
source: Unphosphorylated, active TTP protein is short-lived as TTP targets its own mRNA for rapid decay, resulting in low levels of unphosphorylated TTP that are technically challenging to detect (Brook et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brook et al., 2006.

claim: Any skeletal muscle perturbation such as induced injury or immediate dissection following sacrifice activates satellite cells and p38α/β MAPK.
source: Any skeletal muscle perturbation such as induced injury or immediate dissection following sacrifice, activates SCs and p38α/β MAPK (Jones et al., 2005), which in other cell types, phosphorylates and stabilizes TTP (Tchen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2005 and Tchen et al., 2004.

claim: In uninjured muscle, 50% of the Sdc4+ satellite cells were immunoreactive for TTP and located underneath the basal lamina.
source: In uninjured muscle, 50% of the Sdc4+ SCs were immunoreactive for TTP and located underneath the basal lamina (Figure 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A,B,E.

claim: 1 hr post-injury, the majority of TTP+/Syndecan-4+ cells were located outside of the basal lamina or encased within the basal lamina.
source: In contrast to the uninjured state, 1 hr post-injury we found the majority of TTP+/Syndecan-4+ cells were located outside of the basal lamina or encased within the basal lamina (Figure 2C,E) with a minority present in the SC niche underneath the basal lamina (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C,D,E.

claim: 30 min following a BaCl2 induced injury, substantial muscle damage is evidenced by serum IgG permeable necrotic myofibers.
source: This observation is consistent with substantial muscle damage, as evidenced by serum IgG permeable necrotic myofibers, observed in injured tissue 30 min following a BaCl2 induced injury (Weller et al., 1990) (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F,G and supported by citation to Weller et al., 1990.

claim: 30 min post-injury, 45% of the Syndecan-4+ satellite cells were phospho-MK2 immunoreactive.
source: 30 min post-injury, 45% of the Syndecan-4+ SCs were phospho-MK2 immunoreactive (Figure 3A,B), while uninjured muscle SCs were phospho-MK2 negative (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Phospho-MK2 was significantly reduced if mice were pre-treated with an intraperitoneal injection of SB203580, a p38α/β MAPK inhibitor.
source: Consistent with MK2 activation by p38α/β MAPK, phospho-MK2 was significantly reduced if mice were pre-treated with an intraperitoneal (IP) injection of SB203580, a p38α/β MAPK inhibitor (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Phospho-TTP and HuR were significantly reduced in satellite cells isolated from SB203580 treated mice compared to satellite cells isolated in the absence of the p38α/β MAPK inhibitor.
source: Phospho-TTP and HuR were significantly reduced in SCs isolated from SB203580 treated mice compared to SCs isolated in the absence of the p38α/β MAPK inhibitor, while Syndecan-4 staining remained constant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: In satellite cells, TTP appears to be a p38α/β MAPK target.
source: Thus, in SCs, TTP appears to be a p38α/β MAPK target and pretreating skeletal muscle with a p38α/β MAPK inhibitor reduces TTP phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing that p38α/β MAPK inhibition reduces TTP phosphorylation.

claim: MAPKAPK2 (MK2) is a downstream p38α/β MAPK target regulating TTP in murine macrophage cells.
source: MAPKAPK2 (MK2) is a downstream p38α/β MAPK target regulating TTP in murine macrophage cells (Mahtani et al., 2001; Tiedje et al., 2012; Brooks and Blackshear, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mahtani et al., 2001, Tiedje et al., 2012, and Brooks and Blackshear, 2013.

claim: A robust signal for phospho-MK2::TTP association was observed using proximity ligation assay.
source: A robust signal for phospho-MK2::TTP association using PLA was observed (Figure 3C) and when quantified, was significant compared to contols (Figure 3D), indicating that TTP is a bona-fide p38/MK2 target in SCs and MM14 cells.
evidence: This is shown by PLA data in Figure 3C,D.

claim: TTP is a bona-fide p38/MK2 target in satellite cells and MM14 cells.
source: A robust signal for phospho-MK2::TTP association using PLA was observed (Figure 3C) and when quantified, was significant compared to contols (Figure 3D), indicating that TTP is a bona-fide p38/MK2 target in SCs and MM14 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLA data showing phospho-MK2::TTP association.

claim: Wild-type, vehicle treated myofiber-associated satellite cells uniformly expressed MyoD and were phospho-TTP positive at 24 hr post-isolation.
source: Wild-type, vehicle treated myofiber-associated SCs (Syndecan 4+) uniformly expressed MyoD and were phospho-TTP positive at 24 hr post-isolation, while phospho-TTP was barely detectable in the presence of 10uM MK2 inhibitor III (MK2i, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E.

claim: Phospho-TTP was barely detectable in myofiber-associated satellite cells cultured in the presence of 10uM MK2 inhibitor III.
source: Wild-type, vehicle treated myofiber-associated SCs (Syndecan 4+) uniformly expressed MyoD and were phospho-TTP positive at 24 hr post-isolation, while phospho-TTP was barely detectable in the presence of 10uM MK2 inhibitor III (MK2i, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E.

claim: Concurrent downregulation of MyoD was observed in MK2 inhibitor treated satellite cells.
source: We observed concurrent downregulation of MyoD in the MK2i treated SCs, suggesting that TTP may play a role in p38α/β MAPK-mediated MyoD regulation.
evidence: This is observed in the immunofluorescence data and suggests a role for TTP in MyoD regulation.

claim: The majority (70%) of control transfected satellite cells were MyoD immunoreactive after 30 hr in culture.
source: The majority (70%) of control transfected cells were MyoD immunoreactive (Figure 3F,H), while only 30% of the TTP-AA-myc transfected cells were MyoD immunoreactive (Figure 3G,H), demonstrating that TTP reduces myogenic commitment.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3F,H.

claim: Only 30% of the TTP-AA-myc transfected satellite cells were MyoD immunoreactive after 30 hr in culture.
source: The majority (70%) of control transfected cells were MyoD immunoreactive (Figure 3F,H), while only 30% of the TTP-AA-myc transfected cells were MyoD immunoreactive (Figure 3G,H), demonstrating that TTP reduces myogenic commitment.
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3G,H.

claim: TTP reduces myogenic commitment.
source: The majority (70%) of control transfected cells were MyoD immunoreactive (Figure 3F,H), while only 30% of the TTP-AA-myc transfected cells were MyoD immunoreactive (Figure 3G,H), demonstrating that TTP reduces myogenic commitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced MyoD expression in TTP-AA-myc transfected cells.

claim: Ectopic expression of TTP-AA-myc blocked virtually all satellite cells from inducing MyoD post-transfection.
source: Thus, ectopic expression of TTP-AA-myc blocked virtually all cells from inducing MyoD post-transfection (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is shown by the data in Figure 3H comparing MyoD expression at 6 hr (15%) to 30 hr post-transfection (30%).

claim: MyoD mRNA in skeletal muscle cell lines is stabilized by HuR.
source: MyoD mRNA in skeletal muscle cell lines is stabilized by HuR (van der Giessen et al., 2003) and induction in SCs is concomitant with the loss of TTP (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van der Giessen et al., 2003.

claim: There were no detectable differences in HuR protein expression in control transfected satellite cells as compared to TTP-AA-myc transfected satellite cells.
source: Scoring the percentage of Syndecan-4+ cells that were HuR immunoreactive showed that there were no detectable differences in HuR protein expression in control transfected SCs as compared to TTP-AA-myc transfected SCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: It is unlikely that HuR represents a primary TTP target mRNA in activating satellite cells.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that HuR represents a primary TTP target mRNA in activating SCs and may function to control mRNA stability via an alternative signaling pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing no change in HuR expression with TTP-AA-myc transfection.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis of the MyoD 3′ UTR identified a highly conserved TTP binding site.
source: Bioinformatic analysis of the MyoD 3′ UTR identified a highly conserved TTP binding site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of wild type flag-TTP efficiently co-immunoprecipitated β-MyoD when compared with the negative control β-globin reporter.
source: Immunoprecipitation of wild type flag-TTP efficiently co-immunoprecipitated β-MyoD when compared with the negative control β-globin reporter (β-GAP) (Figure 4A, lane 1), whereas immunoprecipitation of the flag-TTPF162N mutant failed to co-immunoprecipitate β-MyoD (Figure 4A, lane 2).
evidence: This is shown by RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of the flag-TTPF162N mutant failed to co-immunoprecipitate β-MyoD.
source: Immunoprecipitation of wild type flag-TTP efficiently co-immunoprecipitated β-MyoD when compared with the negative control β-globin reporter (β-GAP) (Figure 4A, lane 1), whereas immunoprecipitation of the flag-TTPF162N mutant failed to co-immunoprecipitate β-MyoD (Figure 4A, lane 2).
evidence: This is shown by RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Wild type TTP directly binds the MyoD 3′ UTR.
source: These data demonstrate that wild type TTP directly binds the MyoD 3′ UTR.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA immunoprecipitation data showing co-immunoprecipitation of β-MyoD with wild type TTP but not with the RNA binding mutant.

claim: WTß-MyoD mRNA half-life was 250 min when expressed in Tet-Off Hela cells.
source: WTß-MyoD mRNA half-life was 250 min when expressed in Tet-Off Hela cells (Figure 4C,D), and co-transfection of a construct expressing TTP destabilized the WTß-MyoD mRNA, decreasing mRNA half-life by nearly twofold (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is shown by mRNA decay assay data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Co-transfection of a construct expressing TTP destabilized the WTß-MyoD mRNA, decreasing mRNA half-life by nearly twofold.
source: WTß-MyoD mRNA half-life was 250 min when expressed in Tet-Off Hela cells (Figure 4C,D), and co-transfection of a construct expressing TTP destabilized the WTß-MyoD mRNA, decreasing mRNA half-life by nearly twofold (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is shown by mRNA decay assay data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: TTP-mediated decay of the ß-MyoD mRNA was sensitive to p38α/β MAPK signaling as co-transfection of the TTP construct with a constitutively active MK2 kinase (MK2-EE) increased β-MyoD mRNA stability to ≥350 min.
source: Furthermore, TTP-mediated decay of the ß-MyoD mRNA was sensitive to p38α/β MAPK signaling as co-transfection of the TTP construct with a constitutively active MK2 kinase (MK2-EE) increased β-MyoD mRNA stability to ≥350 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown by mRNA decay assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MyoD mRNA decay was dependent on the predicted TTP binding sequence as mutation of the putative TTP binding sequence rendered TTP incapable of destabilizing MUTβ-MyoD mRNA.
source: MyoD mRNA decay was dependent on the predicted TTP binding sequence as mutation of the putative TTP binding sequence (MUTβ-MyoD; Figure 4B) rendered TTP incapable of destabilizing MUTβ-MyoD mRNA (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is shown by mRNA decay assay data in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Neither the TTP knockout mice nor 3KO mice exhibited any detectable gross morphological differences in muscle sections immunostained with laminin.
source: Neither the TTP knockout mice nor 3KO mice exhibited any detectable gross morphological differences in muscle sections immunostained with laminin (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A.

claim: There were no significant quantitative differences in Pax7+ satellite cells between wild type and knock out muscle sections.
source: Moreover, we did not observe Pax7+ cells outside of the basal lamina (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) nor any significant quantitative differences in Pax7+ SCs between wild type and knock out muscle sections when scoring for Pax7 immunoreactivity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B; additional quantification in Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Extralaminar and sublaminar Ki67+ cells were increased in TTP knockout mice and 3KO mice.
source: In contrast, extralaminar and sublaminar Ki67+ cells were increased in TTP knockout mice and 3KO mice, suggesting that SCs exit the quiescent G0 state in the absence of TTP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Twofold greater numbers of sublaminar MyoD+ cells were observed in TTP knockout mice and in 3KO muscle compared to wild type mice.
source: Consistent with increased myogenic commitment of SCs, we observe twofold greater numbers of sublaminar MyoD+ cells in TTP knockout mice and in 3KO muscle compared to wild type mice (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A,B.

claim: More centrally located nuclei that are indicative of satellite cell fusion into myofibers were present in TTP knockout mice and 3KO mice compared to controls.
source: More centrally located nuclei (CLN) that are indicative of SC fusion into myofibers and a hallmark of muscle injury and repair, were present in TTP knockout mice and 3KO mice compared to controls (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Global loss of TTP appears sufficient to drive a low-level injury response in skeletal muscle in the absence of an overt physical or chemical insult.
source: Thus, global loss of TTP appears sufficient to drive a low-level injury response in skeletal muscle in the absence of an overt physical or chemical insult.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations of increased MyoD+ cells and centrally located nuclei in TTP knockout mice.

claim: A marked increase in mCherry+ fibers was observed in TTP shRNA infected muscle compared to muscle infected with scrambled shRNA expressing virus.
source: A marked increase in mCherry+ fibers was observed in TTP shRNA (shTTPmix) infected muscle compared to muscle infected with scrambled shRNA expressing virus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, right panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: The mCherry+ cells in control muscles infected with the scrambled shRNA expressing RCAS were >95% Pax7+ with fewer than 5% of the mCherry+ cells immunoreactive for MyoD.
source: The mCherry+ cells in control muscles infected with the scrambled shRNA expressing RCAS were >95% Pax7+ with fewer than 5% of the mCherry+ cells immunoreactive for MyoD (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5D-F.

claim: A >threefold increase in MyoD+ immunoreactivity was observed in mCherry+ cells in shTTPmix-infected muscle.
source: In contrast, a >threefold increase in MyoD+ immunoreactivity was observed mCherry+ cells in shTTPmix-infected muscle (Figure 5D,F).
evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5D,F.

claim: Satellite cell-specific TTP knockdown breaks satellite cell quiescence, promoting precocious satellite cell activation and enhancing cell fusion with existing myofibers in the absence of muscle injury.
source: Thus, SC-specific TTP knockdown breaks SC quiescence, promoting precocious SC activation and enhancing cell fusion with existing myofibers in the absence of muscle injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the RCAS-mediated knockdown experiments showing increased MyoD+ cells and mCherry+ fibers.

claim: Relatively constant satellite cell numbers are maintained in healthy adult mice prior to and following single or multiple induced muscle injuries.
source: Relatively constant SC numbers are maintained in healthy adult mice prior to and following single or multiple induced muscle injuries (Cornelison et al., 2004; Pisconti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cornelison et al., 2004 and Pisconti et al., 2010.

claim: miR-489 represses Dek expression to maintain satellite cell quiescence.
source: Elegant experiments have established roles for maintenance of quiescence by microRNAs, where miR-489 represses Dek expression to maintain quiescence, miR-31 represses Myf-5 translation to maintain quiescence, and alternative polyadenylation regulates Pax3 (Boutet et al., 2012; Cheung et al., 2012; Crist et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boutet et al., 2012, Cheung et al., 2012, and Crist et al., 2012.

claim: miR-31 represses Myf-5 translation to maintain satellite cell quiescence.
source: Elegant experiments have established roles for maintenance of quiescence by microRNAs, where miR-489 represses Dek expression to maintain quiescence, miR-31 represses Myf-5 translation to maintain quiescence, and alternative polyadenylation regulates Pax3 (Boutet et al., 2012; Cheung et al., 2012; Crist et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boutet et al., 2012, Cheung et al., 2012, and Crist et al., 2012.

claim: Alternative polyadenylation regulates Pax3.
source: Elegant experiments have established roles for maintenance of quiescence by microRNAs, where miR-489 represses Dek expression to maintain quiescence, miR-31 represses Myf-5 translation to maintain quiescence, and alternative polyadenylation regulates Pax3 (Boutet et al., 2012; Cheung et al., 2012; Crist et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boutet et al., 2012, Cheung et al., 2012, and Crist et al., 2012.

claim: Satellite cell quiescence is actively maintained by mRNA decay via the Tis11 family of RNA binding proteins.
source: Here, we show that in addition to Myf5 and Pax3 (Boutet et al., 2012), MyoD mRNA is regulated post-transcriptionally via a distinct regulatory mechanism whereby MyoD mRNA is targeted for rapid decay in quiescent SCs.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulatory circuitry is required for satellite cell homeostasis and appears to maintain satellite cells in a primed state, permitting a rapid response to skeletal muscle injury.
source: Post-transcriptional regulatory circuitry is required for SC homeostasis and appears to maintain SCs in a primed state, permitting a rapid response to skeletal muscle injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and discussion in the manuscript.

claim: Post-transcriptional gene regulation likely facilitates satellite cell self-renewal by asymmetric division and may regulate satellite cell homeostasis via multiple mechanisms.
source: Moreover, post-transcriptional gene regulation likely facilitates SC self-renewal by asymmetric division and may regulate SC homeostasis via multiple mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings and known mechanisms in the field.

claim: In other tissues undergoing rapid turnover, similar post-transcriptional regulatory networks may ensure that a primed stem cell pool is available to repair and maintain tissue function.
source: In other tissues undergoing rapid turnover, similar post-transcriptional regulatory networks may ensure that a primed stem cell pool is available to repair and maintain tissue function.
evidence: This is a speculative statement extending the findings to other tissue types.

claim: Syndecan-4 null satellite cells are incapable of muscle repair, exhibit severely delayed activation, aberrant MyoD expression, poor growth kinetics, and fail to self-renew.
source: Syndecan-4 null SCs are incapable of muscle repair, exhibit severely delayed activation, aberrant MyoD expression, poor growth kinetics, fail to self-renew (Cornelison et al., 2004; Hall et al., 2010) and thus, transcripts differentially expressed between wildtype and Sdc4−/− SCs may represent genes involved in SC activation and commitment.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cornelison et al., 2004 and Hall et al., 2010.

claim: 70% of RNA binding transcripts in the WT-S4 gene list decreased in wild type satellite cells but did not change in Sdc4−/− satellite cells 12 hr post injury.
source: Transcripts annotated as RNA binding were highly enriched in the WT-S4 gene list (p-value = 8.7e-05) and 70% decreased in wild type SCs but did not change in Sdc4−/− SCs 12 hr post injury.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the figure legend.

claim: The MyoD 3′ UTR TTP binding sequence (TATTTAT) is identical in seven mammals.
source: The MyoD 3′ UTR TTP binding sequence (TATTTAT) is identical in seven mammals as depicted in the UCSC genome browser.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TTP may regulate other mRNAs with AU-rich sites involved in maintenance of satellite cell quiescence.
source: Although MyoD mRNA appears to be a TTP target, TTP likely regulates other mRNAs with AU-rich sites involved in maintenance of SC quiescence.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known function of TTP.

claim: The Tis11 family members Brf1 and Brf2 were also down-regulated upon satellite cell activation.
source: Furthermore, the Tis11 family members Brf1 and Brf2 were also down-regulated upon SC activation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of muscle injury, satellite cell-specific TTP knockdown increased MyoD+ cells, presumably at the expense of Pax7+ progenitor cells.
source: In the absence of muscle injury, SC-specific TTP knockdown increased MyoD+ cells, presumably at the expense of Pax7+ progenitor cells.
evidence: This is shown by the RCAS-mediated knockdown experiments in Figure 5.

claim: The increase in MyoD+ cells was accompanied by an increase in mCherry+ myofibers when compared to controls where satellite cells were infected with scrambled shRNAs.
source: The increase in MyoD+ cells was accompanied by an increase in mCherry+ myofibers when compared to controls where SCs were infected with scrambled shRNAs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: TTP inhibition breaks satellite cell quiescence in uninjured muscle, providing strong evidence for the involvement of TTP in regulating satellite cell homeostasis.
source: Thus, TTP inhibition breaks SC quiescence in uninjured muscle, providing strong evidence for the involvement of TTP in regulating SC homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RCAS-mediated knockdown experiments.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulation of mRNAs by miR-489 maintains satellite cell quiescence.
source: Similarly, post-transcriptional regulation of mRNAs by miR-489 maintains SC quiescence, suggesting Dek and potentially other miR-489 targets regulate SC homeostasis (Cheung et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheung et al., 2012.

claim: It is possible that TTP loss-of-function and miR-489 preferentially affect sub-populations of Pax7+ satellite cells.
source: As we do not know the extent of functional diversity within the Pax7+ SC population it is possible that TTP loss-of-function and miR-489 preferentially affect sub-populations of Pax7+ SCs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging uncertainty about SC heterogeneity.

claim: Satellite cell quiescence is maintained by multiple post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms including miRNA-mediated inhibition of Myf5 translation and Dek translation.
source: SC quiescence is maintained by multiple post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms including miRNA-mediated inhibition of Myf5 translation (Crist et al., 2012) and Dek translation (Cheung et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Crist et al., 2012 and Cheung et al., 2012.

claim: In addition to Myf5 and Pax3, MyoD mRNA is regulated post-transcriptionally via a distinct regulatory mechanism whereby MyoD mRNA is targeted for rapid decay in quiescent satellite cells.
source: Here, we show that in addition to Myf5 and Pax3 (Boutet et al., 2012), MyoD mRNA is regulated post-transcriptionally via a distinct regulatory mechanism whereby MyoD mRNA is targeted for rapid decay in quiescent SCs.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Post-transcriptional regulatory circuitry maintains satellite cells in a primed state, permitting a rapid response to skeletal muscle injury.
source: Post-transcriptional regulatory circuitry is required for SC homeostasis and appears to maintain SCs in a primed state, permitting a rapid response to skeletal muscle injury.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data and discussion in the manuscript.

claim: A total of 5162 unique genes changed when comparing satellite cells isolated from uninjured muscle and muscle 12 hr post-injury in wild type.
source: A total of 5162 and 2236 unique genes changed when comparing satellite cells (SCs) isolated from uninjured muscle and muscle 12 hr post-injury in wild type and Syndecan-4 (Sdc4) null SCs, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the figure legend.

claim: A total of 2236 unique genes changed when comparing satellite cells isolated from uninjured muscle and muscle 12 hr post-injury in Syndecan-4 null satellite cells.
source: A total of 5162 and 2236 unique genes changed when comparing satellite cells (SCs) isolated from uninjured muscle and muscle 12 hr post-injury in wild type and Syndecan-4 (Sdc4) null SCs, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the figure legend.

claim: 1069 genes were common to both wild type and Syndecan-4 null satellite cells when comparing uninjured and 12 hr post-injury.
source: Genes common to both (1069) were subtracted from the wild type gene list yielding 4093 unique genes that changed after injury in wild type but not in Sdc4−/− SCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the figure legend.

claim: 4093 unique genes changed after injury in wild type but not in Sdc4−/− satellite cells.
source: Genes common to both (1069) were subtracted from the wild type gene list yielding 4093 unique genes that changed after injury in wild type but not in Sdc4−/− SCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the figure legend.

claim: 152 total RNA binding genes were identified in the WT-S4 gene list, with 107 (70%) decreasing.
source: Total RNA binding genes: 152; decreased: 107 (70%).
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1B legend.

claim: The abundance of Zfp36l1 and Zfp36l2 transcripts decreased in wild type satellite cells but did not change in Sdc4−/− satellite cells.
source: Abundance of Zfp36l1 and Zfp36l2 transcripts, which encode Brf1 and Brf2, respectively, decreased in wild type satellite cells but did not change in Sdc4−/− satellite cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Brf1 and Brf2 mRNA decreased as satellite cells activated in culture.
source: Brf1 and Brf2 mRNA decreased as satellite cells activated in culture as determined by QT-PCR analysis (means from one representative experiment out of two, each experiment contained five mice; Graphs plotted ± standard deviation. *p-value < 0.01).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of mice with the p38α/β MAPK inhibitor SB203580 and inclusion of SB203580 during satellite cell isolation reduces TTP phosphorylation and HuR induction.
source: Intraperitoneal injection of mice with the p38α/β MAPK inhibitor SB203580 and inclusion of SB203580 during SC isolation reduces TTP phosphorylation and HuR induction.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The percentage of phospho-MK2 positive satellite cells was decreased in the presence of SB203580 following injury (p-value < 0.01 for n = 3).
source: Percentage of phospho-MK2 positive SCs was decreased in the presence of SB203580 following injury. (± SEM * p-value < 0.01 for n = 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The percentage of transfected satellite cells scored for MyoD was plotted for three independent experiments from a minimum 25 myofibers per condition.
source: The percentage of transfected SCs scored for MyoD plotted for three independent experiments from a minimum 25 myofibers per condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3H legend.

claim: The percentage of transfected satellite cells scored for HuR was plotted for two independent experiments from a minimum of 25 myofibers per condition.
source: The percentage of transfected SCs scored for HuR plotted for two independent experiments from a minimum of 25 myofibers per condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 3—figure supplement 1C legend.

claim: The calculated β-MyoD mRNA half-life was determined from the average ± SEM plotted from at least three independent experiments (p = 0.012 for β-MyoD + TTP).
source: The calculated β-MyoD mRNA half-life determined from the average ± SEM plotted from at least three independent experiments. Student's two-tailed t-test; * β-MyoD + TTP, p = 0.012.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 4D legend.

claim: Loss of TTP or combined loss of TTP/TNFR1/2 in muscle results in significant increases in MyoD+ cells.
source: Loss of TTP or combined loss of TTP/TNFR1/2 in muscle results in significant increases in MyoD+ cells (A, B) and centrally located nuclei (quantified in C), both hallmarks of actively regenerating muscle.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A,B,C.

claim: Loss of TTP or combined loss of TTP/TNFR1/2 in muscle results in significant increases in centrally located nuclei.
source: Loss of TTP or combined loss of TTP/TNFR1/2 in muscle results in significant increases in MyoD+ cells (A, B) and centrally located nuclei (quantified in C), both hallmarks of actively regenerating muscle.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A,B,C.

claim: Pax7+ satellite cells were infected with mCherry-tagged shRNAs and analyzed 3 weeks post-infection to examine the effect of TTP knockdown on satellite cell activation.
source: Pax7+ SCs were infected with mCherry-tagged shRNAs and analyzed 3 weeks post-infection to examine the effect of TTP knockdown on SC activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is described in the Figure 5D legend.

claim: When compared to wild type muscle sections, the number of Pax7+ satellite cells were similar in TTP KO and 3KO muscle sections.
source: When compared to WT muscle sections, the number of Pax7+ SCs were similar in TTP KO and 3KO muscle sections.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: TTP loss-of-function results in a significant increase in sublaminar Ki67+ cells.
source: TTP loss-of-function results in a significant increase in sublaminar Ki67+ cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The activation index (mCherry+ fiber/single cell ratio) of control vs TTP knockdown muscle cross-sections 3 weeks post-infection shows a significant difference (p < 0.01).
source: Bar graph depicting the activation index (mCherry+ fiber/single cell ratio) of control vs TTP knockdown muscle cross-sections 3 weeks post-infection. (**) p < 0.01. N = 3 mice for each experimental condition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: TTP suppresses transcripts for satellite cell activation as a mechanism for immediate exit from quiescence.
source: We propose that TTP suppresses transcripts for SC activation as a mechanism for immediate exit from quiescence.
evidence: This is the proposed model shown in Figure 6.

claim: Upon muscle injury, p38α/β MAPK is rapidly activated resulting in phosphorylation of TTP.
source: Upon muscle injury, p38α/β MAPK is rapidly activated resulting in phosphorylation of TTP.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6.

claim: Phospho-TTP no longer suppresses activation-associated transcripts resulting in rapid induction and satellite cell activation.
source: Phospho-TTP no longer suppresses activation-associated transcripts resulting in rapid induction and SC activation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6.

claim: MyoD is rapidly induced due to inactivation of TTP by p38α/β MAPK concurrent with increased MyoD mRNA stability mediated by HuR and transcriptional upregulation of the MyoD gene locus.
source: One such activation-associated transcript targeted by TTP is MyoD, which is rapidly induced due to inactivation of TTP by p38α/β MAPK concurrent with increased MyoD mRNA stability mediated by HuR and transcriptional upregulation of the MyoD gene locus.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6.

claim: Since MyoD up-regulates its own transcription, muscle injury would trigger a rapid feed-forward loop resulting in MyoD expression driving satellite cells to commit to myoblasts.
source: Since MyoD up-regulates its own transcription, muscle injury would trigger a rapid feed-forward loop resulting in MyoD expression driving SCs to commit to myoblasts.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6.

claim: TTP may be involved in down regulation of MyoD mRNA and other TTP-target transcripts expressed by myoblasts, during the initial formation of a quiescent satellite cell population or in reacquisition of quiescence following an injury.
source: Additionally, we propose that TTP may be involved in down regulation of MyoD mRNA and other TTP-target transcripts expressed by myoblasts, during the initial formation of a quiescent SC population or in reacquisition of quiescence following an injury.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 6.
